subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 15 periods = 600 minutes
Total: 15 periods · 10h 0min

periods.activity_title: Idli-Vada: Counting Our Way to Common Multiples

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (Idli-Vada Game), section 5.1 p.107
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students sit in a circle and count aloud; they replace multiples of 3 with 'idli', multiples of 5 with 'vada', and common multiples of both with 'idli-vada'. Players who make a mistake are eliminated. Builds intuition for common multiples through a social game.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: At what number is 'idli-vada' said for the 10th time? (Find the 10th common multiple of 3 and 5.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: If the game is played from 1 to 90, find: (a) how many times 'idli' is said (including 'idli-vada'); (b) how many times 'vada' is said (including 'idli-vada'); (c) how many times 'idli-vada' is said.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.108
homework.description: Is Fig. 5.1 (Venn diagram of multiples of 3 and 5) related to the Idli-Vada game? Draw the figure if the game is played till 60.

time_bands.activity: Launch the Idli-Vada game: the class sits in a circle and counts aloud from 1, substituting 'idli' for multiples of 3, 'vada' for multiples of 5, and 'idli-vada' for common multiples of both. Activity (Idli-Vada Game), section 5.1 p.107 ("replace multiples of 3 with 'idli', multiples of 5 with 'vada'....")

Continue the game with elimination rounds; pause to ask students to list the numbers that triggered 'idli-vada' and circle them on a number strip on the board, surfacing the pattern that common multiples are themselves multiples of 15.

Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q1, section 5.1 p.108 ("At what number is 'idli-vada' said for the 10th time?...") and Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.108 ("how many times 'idli', 'vada', 'idli-vada' said up to 90?..."). Pairs share answers and the class checks together.

Brief class discussion: students articulate in their own words what a common multiple is and why 'idli-vada' numbers are multiples of 15. Assign Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.108 ("Is Fig. 5.1 related to the Idli-Vada game?...") as consolidation work.

periods.teacher_notes: The game works best if students keep a visible tally of 'idli-vada' numbers on the board as play proceeds — this makes the list of common multiples concrete before any formal definition is offered. A common error is treating 15 as the only common multiple rather than recognising that all multiples of 15 also qualify; watch for students who stop listing after 15. The Venn diagram in Fig. 5.1 of the textbook is a useful reference to display once the game data is on the board.
materials: Open floor space or chairs arranged in a circle
Number strip or board grid from 1 to 90
Chalk or markers

periods.activity_title: Jump Jackpot: Landing on Common Factors

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (Jump Jackpot), section 5.1 p.109
textbook_items_in_class.description: Grumpy places treasures on two numbers; Jumpy selects a jump size and can only land on multiples of that size. Students explore which jump sizes reach both treasure numbers, connecting common factors to a game mechanic.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: In Jump Jackpot, treasures are on 28 and 70. What jump sizes land on both numbers?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the common factors of: (a) 20 and 28; (b) 35 and 50; (c) 4, 8 and 12; (d) 5, 15 and 25.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Guna erased numbers from a Venn diagram leaving only the common multiples 24, 48, 72. Find possible values for the two circle labels (the individual multiples regions).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.110
homework.description: Who am I? (a) A number less than 40, one factor is 7, digit sum is 8. (b) A number less than 100, two factors are 3 and 5, one digit is 1 more than the other.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Jump Jackpot scenario: Activity (Jump Jackpot), section 5.1 p.109 ("Grumpy places treasures on two numbers; Jumpy selects a jump size...."). Teacher sets up the problem on the board with treasures at two numbers and students guess which jump sizes would work.

Students work in small groups on Figure it Out Q7, section 5.1 p.111 ("treasures on 28 and 70; what jump sizes land on both?") and Figure it Out Q4, section 5.1 p.111 ("find common factors of given pairs...."). Groups list all factors of each number and identify the overlap.

Groups tackle Figure it Out Q8, section 5.1 p.111 ("common multiples 24, 48, 72 remain; find the two circle labels...."). Discussion surfaces the insight that the GCF is the greatest jump size that reaches both treasures, and that common factors of two numbers are the factors of their GCF.

Class consolidation: students state in their own words the connection between the Jump Jackpot game and common factors. Assign Figure it Out Q2, section 5.1 p.110 ("Who am I? factor and digit-sum clues....") as reinforcement.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse common multiples with common factors; the Jump Jackpot game's directionality (jump size divides the treasure number, not the other way around) is the key corrective. Watch for students who list only one common factor rather than all of them — emphasise that every divisor shared by both numbers qualifies. Having established the Idli-Vada pattern for common multiples, the class is well placed to see the parallel structure here.
materials: Number line drawn on the board (0–80)
Counters or tokens to mark treasure positions
Worksheets with factor tables

periods.activity_title: Venn Diagrams, Puzzles and LCM Connections

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: Play the Idli-Vada game with different number pairs — (a) 2 and 5, (b) 3 and 7, (c) 4 and 6 — and draw Venn diagrams like Fig. 5.1 for each pair up to 60.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.108
textbook_items_in_class.description: One number in an Idli-Vada game was 4 and nobody ever said just 'vada'. Which of 2, 3, 5, 8, 10 could be the other number?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: Anshu plays Idli-Vada with two numbers both smaller than 10. The first 'idli-vada' comes after number 50. What could the two numbers be?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.111
textbook_items_in_class.description: A perfect number equals the sum of all its factors divided by 2. Given that 28 is perfect, find a perfect number between 1 and 10.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.111
homework.description: Find the smallest number that is a multiple of all numbers from 1 to 10, except 7. (Try This)

time_bands.activity: Students draw Venn diagrams for three number pairs using Figure it Out Q5, section 5.1 p.108 ("play Idli-Vada with (2,5), (3,7), (4,6) and draw Venn diagrams...."). They compare first common multiples: 10, 21, 12 — prompting the question of when LCM equals the product.

Class works through Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.108 ("one number is 4; nobody says just 'vada'; which other numbers work?...") and Figure it Out Q6, section 5.1 p.111 ("first 'idli-vada' after 50 with both numbers under 10...."). Students notice that a large first common multiple implies numbers with no small shared multiples.

Introduce the perfect number idea via Figure it Out Q3, section 5.1 p.111 ("sum of all factors ÷ 2 equals the number; find perfect number between 1 and 10...."). Students list factors of small numbers systematically, reinforcing factor-finding skill.

Class summarises what the three Venn diagrams revealed about LCM and the product of two numbers. Assign Figure it Out Q9, section 5.1 p.111 ("smallest multiple of all numbers 1–10 except 7....") as an extension challenge.

periods.teacher_notes: The comparison of pairs (2,5), (3,7) and (4,6) in Q5 is productive precisely because the first two pairs have LCM equal to their product while (4,6) does not; guide students to articulate why. Students may struggle with the perfect number definition in Q3 — verify that 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28, and that 28 ÷ 2 = 14 would be incorrect framing; the definition says the number equals the sum of all its factors other than itself. Watch for factor-listing errors that skip 1 or the number itself.
materials: Graph paper or printed Venn diagram outlines
Coloured pencils
Factor tables for reference

periods.activity_title: Rectangular Arrays and the Birth of Primes

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there any even prime other than 2?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of the following numbers are prime: 23, 51, 37, 26?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify whether each statement is true or false and explain: (a) no prime has units digit 4; (b) a product of primes can be prime; (c) primes have no factors; (d) all even numbers are composite; (e) for every prime other than 2, the next number is composite.

time_bands.activity: Students use square tiles (or grid paper) to form all possible rectangular arrangements for each number from 1 to 12. They record how many distinct rectangles each number allows, building a factor-count table on the board.

From the table, class identifies which numbers permit exactly two rectangles (1×n and n×1 only). Teacher introduces the textbook's Guna–Anshu narrative about 12 figs versus 7 figs, then formally defines prime (exactly two distinct factors: 1 and itself), composite (more than two factors), and the special status of 1 (neither). Figure it Out Q1, section 5.2 p.114 ("Is there any even prime other than 2?") is discussed as a class.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q4, section 5.2 p.114 ("which of 23, 51, 37, 26 are prime?") then discuss Figure it Out Q9, section 5.2 p.114 ("true or false: no prime has units digit 4; a product of primes can be prime; primes have no factors...."). Pairs write down their reasoning before sharing.

Class formulates a one-sentence definition of a prime number in their own words. Teacher notes that 1 being excluded from both categories is a deliberate mathematical choice, and previews the Sieve as a way to find all primes up to 100 systematically.

periods.teacher_notes: The rectangular-array approach grounds the abstract definition in something students can see and count; insist that a 3×4 and a 4×3 rectangle count as different arrangements to keep the factor-count meaningful. A common error in Q9(c) is interpreting 'no factors' to mean 'no factors other than 1 and itself' — the correct answer is false, since every number including primes has at least two factors. Students who assert that 1 is prime should be redirected to the definition: 1 has only one distinct factor, so it fails the 'exactly two' condition.
materials: Square tiles or 1 cm grid paper
Printed number grid 1–12
Board space for factor-count table

periods.activity_title: The Sieve of Eratosthenes: Pattern-Hunting to 100

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the list of primes up to 100, what is the smallest difference between two successive primes? What is the largest difference?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Are there an equal number of primes in every row of the sieve table? Which decades have the fewest primes? Which have the most?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Twin primes differ by 2. Find all twin prime pairs between 1 and 100.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find seven consecutive composite numbers between 1 and 100.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.115
homework.description: 3 is prime and 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 is also prime. Find at least five other primes p for which 2p + 1 is also prime.

time_bands.activity: Students work with a printed 10×10 grid (numbers 1–100). Following the Sieve instructions from the textbook: circle 2 and cross out all subsequent multiples of 2; circle 3 and cross out all subsequent multiples of 3; continue with 5, 7. All surviving circled numbers are prime. Students compare their completed sieves with a partner.

Students use their completed sieve to answer Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.114 ("smallest and largest differences between successive primes...") and Figure it Out Q3, section 5.2 p.114 ("equal primes per decade? which rows have most and fewest?..."). Class discusses the Math Talk prompt from the textbook: why does crossing out multiples of 2, 3, 5, and 7 suffice for primes up to 100?

Students investigate Figure it Out Q8, section 5.2 p.114 ("find all twin prime pairs between 1 and 100...") and Figure it Out Q7, section 5.2 p.114 ("find seven consecutive composite numbers...."). Partners share their lists and reconcile any differences.

Brief class debrief: students articulate why the sieve is more reliable than checking primes one by one, and offer one conjecture of their own about primes. Assign Figure it Out Q12, section 5.2 p.115 ("find five primes p where 2p + 1 is also prime....") as investigative homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The key reasoning moment is the Math Talk question about why stopping at 7 suffices — guide students to see that any composite ≤ 100 must have a prime factor ≤ 10 (since √100 = 10), so primes 2, 3, 5, 7 cover everything. A common error is crossing out 2 itself when striking out multiples; emphasise that only numbers after 2 are struck. The historical note about Eratosthenes is worth a brief mention to contextualise systematic method-making.
materials: Printed 10×10 number grids (1–100) per student
Coloured pencils or markers (two colours)
Class display of completed sieve for comparison

periods.activity_title: Prime Patterns: Digit Reversals, Composites and Products

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write three pairs of prime numbers less than 20 whose sum is a multiple of 5.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.2 p.114
textbook_items_in_class.description: The numbers 13 and 31 are prime and use the same digits. Find other such digit-reversal prime pairs up to 100.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of 45, 60, 91, 105, 330 is the product of exactly three distinct prime numbers?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 5.2 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many three-digit prime numbers can you make using each of 2, 4 and 5 exactly once?

time_bands.activity: Students recall their sieve from the previous unit and work on Figure it Out Q5, section 5.2 p.114 ("three pairs of primes under 20 whose sum is a multiple of 5...") and Figure it Out Q6, section 5.2 p.114 ("digit-reversal prime pairs up to 100...."). Students share pairs and look for a pattern in which reversal pairs exist.

Class tackles Figure it Out Q10, section 5.2 p.115 ("which of 45, 60, 91, 105, 330 is a product of exactly three distinct primes?..."). Students factorise each candidate and count distinct prime factors. Builds towards prime factorisation by factoring slightly larger numbers through trial division.

Students investigate Figure it Out Q11, section 5.2 p.115 ("how many three-digit primes use 2, 4, 5 exactly once?..."). They list all six arrangements (245, 254, 425, 452, 524, 542) and check each for primality. Class discusses why even numbers and multiples of 5 are immediately ruled out.

Quick class consolidation: students state one reasoning rule they used today (e.g., 'no even number above 2 can be prime') and explain why it is true. Teacher ties this back to the definition of prime numbers.

periods.teacher_notes: Q11 is particularly rich for reasoning: students should recognise before checking that any arrangement ending in 2, 4, or 5 is immediately non-prime, leaving only 425 (= 5 × 85, not prime) and 245 (= 5 × 49, not prime) to eliminate — so the answer is zero. Watch for students who test all six without first applying the last-digit rule. In Q10, students may need prompting that 'three distinct primes' means three different prime bases, not three prime factors (so 2² × 3 does not qualify).
materials: Completed sieve grids from previous unit or a shared class display
Worksheets with Q10 and Q11
Calculators for verification (optional)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.3 p.115
textbook_items_in_class.description: Check if each pair is 'safe' (co-prime): (a) 15 and 39; (b) 4 and 15; (c) 18 and 29; (d) 20 and 55.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.3 p.116
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of the following pairs are co-prime: (a) 18 and 35; (b) 15 and 37; (c) 30 and 415; (d) 17 and 69; (e) 81 and 18?

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-introduces the treasure-game scenario from section 5.3: jump size 1 is now forbidden, so Grumpy must choose treasure positions that no single jump size ≥ 2 can reach both. Students predict which pairs of numbers would be 'safe' and explain their reasoning before any definition is given.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 5.3 p.115 ("check if (15,39), (4,15), (18,29), (20,55) are safe/co-prime..."). They list factors of each number, find common factors, and decide whether the only shared factor is 1. Class records results in a table.

Students extend to Figure it Out Q2, section 5.3 p.116 ("which of (18,35), (15,37), (30,415), (17,69), (81,18) are co-prime?..."). After completing the table, class formulates the definition: two numbers are co-prime if and only if their only common factor is 1. Teacher notes that co-prime numbers need not themselves be prime.
Students give two examples of co-prime pairs where neither number is prime, reinforcing that co-primality is a relational property, not a property of either number alone. Brief class share-out.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent confusion is between 'prime' and 'co-prime': emphasise that 4 and 9 are co-prime even though both are composite. Students may initially check only one or two factors rather than listing all factors of both numbers; encourage systematic listing before they look for overlaps. Having worked through common factors in section 5.1, students already have the tools — this unit names the special case where the GCF is 1.
materials: Factor-listing worksheets
Number line or 100-chart for reference
Board table for recording results

periods.activity_title: Co-prime Art: Thread Patterns Around Pegs

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity (Co-prime Art), section 5.3 p.116
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students observe and analyse thread-art diagrams with different peg counts and thread-gaps. They predict which combinations visit all pegs (co-prime pairs) versus only some pegs (non-co-prime pairs) and create their own diagrams for four specified peg/gap combinations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 5.3 p.116
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find examples where the LCM equals the product of the two numbers, and examples where LCM is less than the product. How is this related to the pair being co-prime?

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays thread-art diagrams from Activity (Co-prime Art), section 5.3 p.116 ("predict which peg/gap combinations visit all pegs versus only some...."). Students predict for four combinations before drawing, recording their guess (co-prime or not) and the reasoning.

Students draw their own thread-art diagrams for the four specified peg/gap combinations on dot-paper circles. They track which pegs are visited and check whether their prediction matched the result. Groups compare diagrams and identify the pattern: all pegs visited if and only if peg count and gap are co-prime.

Class discusses the Math Talk prompt at section 5.3 p.116 ("when does LCM equal the product; how does this connect to co-primality?..."). Students use the examples from Q1–Q2 of the earlier unit to generate evidence: (4,15), LCM = 60 = 4 × 15; (20,55), LCM = 220 < 20 × 55.

Students state the conclusion in their own words: when two numbers are co-prime, their LCM equals their product. Teacher links this back to the Idli-Vada game — when the two game numbers are co-prime, the first 'idli-vada' equals their product.

periods.teacher_notes: The visual impact of the thread-art activity is strongest when students draw at least two contrasting cases — one co-prime pair and one non-co-prime pair — before discussing the pattern. Watch for students who draw the diagrams correctly but cannot articulate why visiting all pegs relates to the GCF; prompt them to count how many pegs are visited and compare that to GCF(peg count, gap). The LCM–product connection in the Math Talk rewards students who recall the Venn diagrams from section 5.1.
materials: Dot-paper circles (or printed peg diagrams) with 6, 8, 9, 12 pegs
Coloured pencils or fine-tip markers
Ruler for drawing straight thread lines

periods.activity_title: Why Ad Hoc Fails: The Need for Prime Factorisation

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.120
Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: A number's prime factorisation has one 2, two 3s, and one 11. What is the number?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.4 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the smallest number whose prime factorisation has: (a) three different prime numbers; (b) four different prime numbers?

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the Anshu–Guna dialogue: Anshu writes 56 = 14 × 4 and declares that 56 and 63 share no common factor. Guna spots an error. Students are asked to find the flaw — they discover that 14 = 2 × 7, and 63 = 9 × 7, so 7 is a common factor that the incomplete factorisation hid.

Teacher demonstrates prime factorisation of 36 using a tree diagram in two different ways (36 = 4 × 9 and 36 = 6 × 6) and shows both produce 2² × 3². Uniqueness of prime factorisation is stated. Students practice with Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.120 ("find prime factorisations of 64, 104, 105, 243, 320...."), working in pairs.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.120 ("one 2, two 3s, one 11 — what is the number?...") working backwards from the factorisation. Then Figure it Out Q5, section 5.4 p.120 ("smallest number with three distinct primes; four distinct primes?...") — students identify 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 and 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 210.

Class reasons through the uniqueness claim: could two different prime factorisations ever describe the same number? Students offer attempts to build a counterexample, guided to see that any 'different' factorisation must include a repeated or composite factor, not a distinct prime product.

periods.teacher_notes: The opening dialogue is the conceptual hinge: ensure students see that 56 = 14 × 4 is a valid factorisation but not a prime factorisation, and that missing a prime factor (7) leads to an incorrect co-primality conclusion. A common error in the tree diagram is stopping at a composite branch — check that students continue factoring until every leaf is prime. The 'number of primes' questions in Q5 reward students who recognise that using the smallest available primes (2, 3, 5, 7) minimises the product.
materials: Blank factor-tree templates
Board space for tree diagram demonstration
Calculators for checking larger factorisations (optional)

periods.activity_title: Prime Factorisation for Co-primality and Divisibility

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Are the following pairs co-prime? Guess first, then verify using prime factorisation: (a) 30 and 45; (b) 57 and 85; (c) 121 and 1331; (d) 343 and 216.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the first number divisible by the second? Use prime factorisation: (a) 225 and 27; (b) 96 and 24; (c) 343 and 17; (d) 999 and 99.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: First number has prime factorisation 2 × 3 × 7; second has 3 × 7 × 11. Are they co-prime? Does one divide the other?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.4 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: Guna says any two prime numbers are co-prime. Is he right?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.4 p.120
homework.description: Find three prime numbers, all less than 30, whose product is 1955.

time_bands.activity: Students work through Example, section 5.4 p.120 ("check if 40 and 231 are co-prime using prime factorisation...") and Example, section 5.4 p.121 ("check if 242 and 195 are co-prime....") as teacher-guided walkthroughs before turning to the exercise set.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.122 ("guess then verify co-primality of (30,45), (57,85), (121,1331), (343,216)...."). They record a gut-feel prediction, then compute prime factorisations and compare prime factor lists. Class discusses which guesses were correct and why.

Students apply divisibility-via-factorisation to Figure it Out Q2, section 5.4 p.122 ("is first divisible by second? use prime factorisation for (225,27), (96,24), (343,17), (999,99)....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 5.4 p.122 ("two factorisations given; are they co-prime; does one divide other?..."). Students articulate the rule: A is divisible by B if and only if every prime in B's factorisation appears at least as many times in A's.

Figure it Out Q4, section 5.4 p.122 ("Guna: any two primes are co-prime — is he right?...") is discussed as a class. Students verify with examples and state why distinct primes share no common factor other than 1. Assign Figure it Out Q3, section 5.4 p.120 ("three primes under 30 whose product is 1955....") as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The key conceptual step is the bridge from co-primality (no shared prime) to divisibility (every prime of the divisor is present with sufficient multiplicity in the dividend); students often conflate these two tests. Watch for errors in Q2(a): 225 = 3² × 5² and 27 = 3³ — 27 requires three 3s but 225 has only two, so 225 is not divisible by 27. The worked examples in the textbook at p.120–122 provide models that students can consult if they lose the procedure.
materials: Factor-tree templates
Worked-example reference cards (p.120–122)
Board space for live factorisation demonstrations

periods.activity_title: Last Digits and Patterns: Deriving Divisibility Rules

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.5 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the remainders when 78, 99, 173, 572, 980, 1111, 2345 are each divided by (a) 10, (b) 5, (c) 2.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 5.5 p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore whether each statement is always, sometimes, or never true: (a) sum of two even numbers is a multiple of 4; (b) sum of two odd numbers is a multiple of 4.

time_bands.activity: Students list the first 20 multiples of 10, 5, and 2 in a table and circle the units digit of each. They state the last-digit pattern for each divisor: multiples of 10 end in 0; multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5; multiples of 2 end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Teacher confirms via the Math Talk reasoning from the textbook.

Students work on Figure it Out Q4, section 5.5 p.126 ("remainders when 78, 99, 173, 572, 980, 1111, 2345 are divided by 10, 5, 2...."). They record answers without long division, using only the last digit. Discuss: the remainder when dividing by 10, 5, or 2 is fully determined by the units digit.

Teacher presents the divisibility-by-4 puzzle: 12 and 22 have the same units digit but only 12 is divisible by 4. Students explore multiples of 4 up to 100 and identify which last two digits appear. The three textbook statements about the last-two-digit rule are presented and students discuss whether each is equivalent to divisibility by 4. Students tackle Figure it Out Q3, section 5.5 p.125 ("always/sometimes/never: sum of two even numbers is a multiple of 4....").

Class reasons about why one digit suffices for 2 and 5 but two digits are needed for 4. Teacher states the analogous rule for 8 (last three digits) and previews why the same logic applies. Students write the three rules in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The conceptual shift from one-digit to two-digit tests is the most important step in this unit; ensure students see that it is the last two digits that form a two-digit number whose divisibility by 4 determines the whole number's divisibility. A common error in Q3 is giving only examples rather than a general argument — prompt students to try pairs like (2+2), (4+4), (2+4) to see that 'sometimes' is the correct classification. The Math Talk verification of the three equivalent statements for the two-digit rule builds deductive reasoning.
materials: Multiples tables (10, 5, 2, 4) printed or on board
Worksheets for Q3 and Q4

periods.activity_title: Leap Years, Palindromes and the Power of Two Checks

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.5 p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: 2024 is a leap year. Leap years are multiples of 4, except multiples of 100 that are not multiples of 400. (a) From your birth year to now, which years were leap years? (b) From 2024 to 2099, how many leap years are there?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.5 p.125
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the largest and smallest 4-digit numbers that are both divisible by 4 and palindromes.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 5.5 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: The teacher asked if 14560 is divisible by all of 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10. Guna checked only two of these numbers and declared divisibility by all. What could those two numbers be?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 5.5 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of 572, 2352, 5600, 6000, 77622160 are divisible by all of 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 5.5 p.126
homework.description: Write two numbers whose product is 10000, where neither number has 0 as its units digit.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 5.5 p.125 ("2024 is a leap year; which years in your lifetime were leap years; how many from 2024 to 2099?..."). They apply the combined divisibility rule (multiple of 4, with exceptions for multiples of 100 unless also multiples of 400) and count carefully.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 5.5 p.125 ("largest and smallest 4-digit palindromes divisible by 4...."). A palindrome ABBA has last two digits BA; students enumerate which two-digit palindromic endings (e.g., 11, 22, 33 …) are divisible by 4 and identify the largest and smallest full palindromes.

Students reason through Figure it Out Q5, section 5.5 p.126 ("which two numbers did Guna check to confirm divisibility by all five?...") and Figure it Out Q6, section 5.5 p.126 ("which of the given numbers are divisible by all five?...."). Discussion establishes that checking 8 and 5 (or 8 and 10) suffices because divisibility by 8 implies divisibility by 4 and by 2.

Assign Figure it Out Q7, section 5.5 p.126 ("two numbers with product 10000, neither ending in 0....") as homework — this rewards students who use prime factorisation of 10000 = 2⁴ × 5⁴ and distribute factors to avoid a trailing zero.

periods.teacher_notes: The leap-year problem is an excellent opportunity for compound logical reasoning — students must hold three rules simultaneously. The palindrome problem in Q2 is a good differentiation task: weaker students can work on 4-digit palindromes systematically while stronger students can explain why only even palindromic endings can be divisible by 4. In Q5, watch for the misconception that checking 2 and 4 is sufficient — this misses divisibility by 5, and students need to realise that 5 and 8 have no divisibility relationship.
materials: Calendars or year-list for the leap-year problem
Palindrome exploration worksheet
Number line or hundreds chart for pattern verification

periods.activity_title: Divisibility by 8: Three-Digit Rules and Reasoning

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.4 p.120
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the prime factorisation without multiplying first: (a) 56 × 25; (b) 108 × 75; (c) 1000 × 81.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.5 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the remainders when 78, 99, 173, 572, 980, 1111, 2345 are each divided by (a) 10, (b) 5, (c) 2.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the reasoning chain: divisibility by 4 depends on the last two digits because 100 is a multiple of 4, so any number = 100k + (last two digits) and 100k is always divisible by 4. Students extend this logic: 1000 is a multiple of 8, so divisibility by 8 depends only on the last three digits. Students verify with three examples from the number list.

Students apply the last-three-digit rule for divisibility by 8 to the numbers in Figure it Out Q4, section 5.5 p.126 ("remainders when numbers are divided by 10, 5, 2....") and then extend to the numbers in Q6 (572, 2352, 5600, 6000, 77622160) checking which are divisible by 8. Class compares the last-three-digit extraction method with the full division method.

Students work on Figure it Out Q4, section 5.4 p.120 ("prime factorisation of 56 × 25, 108 × 75, 1000 × 81 without multiplying first...."). This connects divisibility reasoning back to prime factorisation: 1000 × 81 = 2³ × 5³ × 3⁴, making divisibility by 8 (= 2³) immediately visible.

Students summarise all five divisibility rules (10, 5, 2, 4, 8) in a single table and note which rule implies which: divisibility by 8 implies divisibility by 4 which implies divisibility by 2. Teacher notes that rules for 3, 6, 7, and 9 involve digit sums and will appear in later classes.

periods.teacher_notes: The deductive chain — 100 is divisible by 4, so last two digits determine divisibility by 4; 1000 is divisible by 8, so last three digits determine divisibility by 8 — is the most important piece of reasoning this unit develops. Students who do not see why 100k is always divisible by 4 should be asked to factor 100 = 2² × 5² and note that 4 = 2² divides it. The Q4 exercise with products serves as a useful bridge between prime factorisation (section 5.4) and the divisibility tests — students realise they can read divisibility directly from a factorisation.
materials: Summary divisibility-rules table (blank for students to fill)
Worked examples from textbook p.125–126 as reference
Board space for the deductive reasoning chain

periods.activity_title: Special Numbers: Every Number Has a Story

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk (Special Numbers), section 5.6 p.126
textbook_items_in_class.description: In each box of four numbers, explain how each number is special compared to the others. Share and compare reasons with classmates. Boxes include: {9, 16, 25, 43}; {5, 7, 3, 8}; {27, 3, 17, 27}; {12, 35, 11, 24}; {123, 31, 44, 65}.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the first box {9, 16, 25, 43} from Math Talk (Special Numbers), section 5.6 p.126 ("explain what makes each number special compared to the others...."). Students brainstorm individually for two minutes, then a few responses are shared — establishing that the same number can be special for multiple reasons.

Small groups each take one of the remaining boxes ({5, 7, 3, 8}; {27, 3, 17, 27}; {12, 35, 11, 24}; {123, 31, 44, 65}) and prepare at least two distinct valid reasons why each number in their box is special. Groups draw on all chapter concepts: prime, composite, co-prime, perfect square, divisibility, prime factorisation.

Groups present their boxes to the class. For each number, multiple groups share different valid reasons. Class debates whether a reason is truly valid and checks using chapter methods (e.g., test primality, compute prime factorisation, check divisibility).

Students individually write down one number of their own choosing and state two reasons why it is special, using chapter vocabulary. This serves as a quick informal assessment of conceptual recall across the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The open-ended nature of this activity is intentional — resist the urge to validate only one 'correct' reason per number. Students who identify 43 as both the only prime and the only non-perfect-square in {9, 16, 25, 43} are demonstrating genuine synthesis. A common error is giving superficial reasons ('it is the biggest') that do not use number-theoretic properties; redirect such students by asking whether their reason uses any concept from the chapter. The box {27, 3, 17, 27} contains a repeated number — this is deliberate and worth discussing.
materials: Printed cards or board display of the five number boxes
Blank paper for group brainstorming
Chapter vocabulary reference list (prime, composite, co-prime, LCM, GCF, prime factorisation, perfect square)

periods.activity_title: Prime Puzzle: Constraints, Grids and Creative Search

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk (Prime Puzzle), section 5.6 p.127
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill grids with prime numbers so that the product of each row equals the number to its right and the product of each column equals the number below it. Two grids provided (3×3 and larger). Sub-parts: (a) solve the first puzzle; (b) solve the second larger puzzle.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Prime Puzzle from Math Talk (Prime Puzzle), section 5.6 p.127 ("fill grids with primes; row products equal numbers on right; column products equal numbers below...."). Students read the first grid, note the row and column product constraints, and discuss what the prime factorisation of each product must look like.

Students work individually or in pairs on the first grid (sub-part a). Strategy: compute the prime factorisation of each row product, then ask which prime factors can satisfy the column product simultaneously. Students record their working and test candidate primes systematically.

Students attempt the larger second grid (sub-part b). Pairs compare partial solutions and reason about which cells are overconstrained. Class discusses strategies: filling rows where the product is a prime power first reduces ambiguity. Teacher circulates and prompts with questions rather than corrections.

Class debrief: students name one strategy that helped them make progress and one place where they were stuck. Teacher highlights that the puzzle has a unique solution because the combined row and column constraints leave no free choice — a preview of constraint-satisfaction thinking.

periods.teacher_notes: The Prime Puzzle is a genuine problem-solving experience: students who attempt to guess and check without using prime factorisation will quickly run out of moves, so the lesson concretely demonstrates the power of the chapter's central tool. Watch for students who confuse 'product of row = number on right' with 'sum'; make the distinction concrete with the first row before releasing students to work independently. Students who finish early can be challenged to design their own valid Prime Puzzle grid — a task that requires working backwards from a chosen set of prime entries.
materials: Printed Prime Puzzle grids from section 5.6 p.127
Scrap paper for prime factorisation working
Board space for class strategy discussion

items.prompt: In the Idli-Vada game, a player says 'idli-vada' whenever a number is a common multiple of both 3 and 5. Which of the following numbers would make a player say 'idli-vada'?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 30. It is a multiple of both 3 (30 ÷ 3 = 10) and 5 (30 ÷ 5 = 6), so it is a common multiple of 3 and 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check each option for divisibility by both 3 and 5; only 30 satisfies both conditions.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student identified a multiple of 3 and 7 but confused multiples of 7 with multiples of 5.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly states the definition of a prime number?

options.label: A
options.text: A number greater than 1 that is not a perfect square

options.label: B
options.text: A number that cannot be divided by 2

options.label: C
options.text: A number that has exactly two distinct factors: 1 and itself

options.label: D
options.text: A number that has no factors at all

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A prime number has exactly two distinct factors: 1 and itself.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the definition from the rectangular-array reasoning: primes are numbers that can only be arranged in a single 1 × n rectangle.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses 'prime' with a number having no factors, forgetting that every number has at least 1 and itself as factors.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is recalling the definition of an odd number, not a prime number; 2 itself is the only even prime.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is confusing primality with another property; many primes are not perfect squares, but that is not the defining criterion.

inclusivity.support: Check the definition by looking back at the Guna–Anshu fig-arranging story: what made 7 different from 12?
inclusivity.challenge: Give an example of a number that is odd and composite (not prime), and explain why it does not fit the prime definition.

items.prompt: Two numbers are called co-prime if their only common factor is 1. Which of the following pairs is co-prime?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8 and 15 are co-prime. Factors of 8: 1, 2, 4, 8. Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. The only shared factor is 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all factors of each number in the pair and identify common factors; co-prime means the only common factor is 1.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student did not check factors carefully; 12 and 18 share factors 1, 2, 3, 6.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have noticed both are even-adjacent numbers, but 6 and 9 share the factor 3.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have noticed neither is a multiple of the other, but 14 and 21 share the factor 7.

inclusivity.support: Write out the full factor list of each number side by side and circle the numbers that appear in both lists.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a pair of composite numbers that are co-prime and explain why composites can still be co-prime.

items.prompt: Priya says: 'I crossed out all multiples of 2, 3, 5, and 7 from a 1–100 grid (keeping 2, 3, 5, and 7 themselves). Every number that remained must be prime.' Is Priya correct? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is correct. Any composite number up to 100 must have a prime factor that is at most the square root of 100, which is 10. The only primes up to 10 are 2, 3, 5, and 7. Therefore, every composite number up to 100 has at least one of 2, 3, 5, or 7 as a factor and will be crossed out. Any number that survives is not divisible by any of these four primes, so it can have no prime factor ≤ 10, meaning it can have no composite structure at all — it must be prime.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes reasoning: every composite ≤ 100 has a prime factor ≤ √100 = 10, and the only primes ≤ 10 are 2, 3, 5, 7.

inclusivity.support: Try listing a few composites between 50 and 100 (like 51, 57, 77) and check which of 2, 3, 5, 7 divides each one to see why crossing out those multiples is enough.
inclusivity.challenge: What is the smallest number of primes you would need to cross out to find all primes up to 200? Explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 5.2 p.114

items.prompt: Rajan claims that the sum of any two prime numbers is always even. Is he right? Justify your answer with a clear explanation, not just an example.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rajan is not always right. Every prime other than 2 is odd (since an even number greater than 2 has 2 as a factor and is therefore composite). The sum of two odd numbers is always even, so the sum of any two primes both greater than 2 is even. However, 2 is prime and odd is prime, and 2 + 3 = 5, which is odd. So the sum of two primes is even unless one of them is 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the fact that 2 is the only even prime; the sum of two odd numbers is even, but adding 2 (even) to any odd prime gives an odd sum.

inclusivity.support: Think about whether all primes are odd first — then consider what happens when you add two odd numbers versus one odd and one even.
inclusivity.challenge: Change Rajan's claim to make it always true — write a corrected version of his statement and explain why your version works.

items.prompt: Mia says: 'I factorised 84 as 84 = 4 × 21, so I know all its factors.' Her classmate Dev says that Mia's factorisation is incomplete and she might miss a common factor when comparing 84 with another number. Who is right, and why? Use the idea of prime factorisation to support your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Dev is right. Writing 84 = 4 × 21 is a valid factorisation but not a prime factorisation, because both 4 and 21 are composite. The complete prime factorisation is 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. If Mia only looks at the factors 4 and 21, she might conclude that 84 shares no factor with a number like 28. But 28 = 2 × 2 × 7, and the prime factorisation of 84 clearly shows they share factors 2 and 7. A complete prime factorisation reveals every prime building block, ensuring no common factor is missed.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Continue factorising until every factor is prime; only the complete prime factorisation guarantees that all shared prime factors are visible.

inclusivity.support: Draw a factor tree for 84 stopping at 4 × 21, then continue until every branch ends in a prime number and compare the two trees.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a specific second number whose common factors with 84 would be missed if only the 4 × 21 factorisation were used, and explain precisely which common prime factor is hidden.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.120

items.prompt: A student says: 'To check if a number is divisible by 4, I only need to look at the last digit.' Is this correct? Explain why or why not, using the numbers 12 and 32 as part of your explanation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student is incorrect. The last digit alone is not enough to determine divisibility by 4. For example, 12 and 32 both end in 2, but 12 ÷ 4 = 3 (divisible) while 32 ÷ 4 = 8 (also divisible) — yet 22 also ends in 2 and 22 ÷ 4 = 5 remainder 2 (not divisible). A better approach is to look at the last two digits: any number equals a multiple of 100 plus its last two digits, and since 100 is divisible by 4, divisibility by 4 depends entirely on whether the last two digits form a number divisible by 4. 12 and 32 are both divisible by 4; 22 is not.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the fact that 100 is divisible by 4, so only the last two digits determine divisibility by 4.

inclusivity.support: List five 2-digit numbers ending in 2 and check each for divisibility by 4 to see that the last digit alone is not a reliable rule.
inclusivity.challenge: Explain in one sentence why the same last-two-digit logic extends to give a last-three-digit rule for divisibility by 8.

Common multiples less than 100: 36 and 72. The LCM is 36 and all common multiples are multiples of 36.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of each number and identify the smallest common value, then note that all common multiples are multiples of that LCM.

Common multiples (LCM = 12): 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. These 5 numbers go in the intersection. 'Idli-vada' is said 5 times. Numbers only in the multiples-of-4 region: 4, 8, 16, 20, 28, 32, 40, 44, 52, 56. items.prompt: In a thread-art diagram, there are 10 pegs arranged in a circle numbered 0 to 9. A thread is wound by jumping a fixed gap each time (e.g., a gap of 3 means: peg 0 → peg 3 → peg 6 → peg 9 → peg 2 → …). For each of the following gaps, state whether every peg is visited before the thread returns to peg 0, and explain why: (a) gap = 3, (b) gap = 7.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Gap = 3, pegs = 10. GCF(10, 3) = 1 since 10 = 2 × 5 and 3 is prime with no shared factor. Because 10 and 3 are co-prime, every peg is visited exactly once before returning to peg 0. The sequence visits all 10 pegs: 0, 3, 6, 9, 2, 5, 8, 1, 4, 7, 0. (b) Gap = 7, pegs = 10. GCF(10, 7) = 1 since 10 = 2 × 5 and 7 is prime with no shared factor. Because 10 and 7 are co-prime, every peg is also visited exactly once. The sequence: 0, 7, 4, 1, 8, 5, 2, 9, 6, 3, 0.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find GCF(peg count, gap); if GCF = 1 (co-prime), every peg is visited; if GCF > 1, only peg count ÷ GCF pegs are visited.

inclusivity.support: Draw 10 pegs in a circle and physically trace the path for gap = 3, marking each visited peg, to see whether all 10 are reached.
inclusivity.challenge: For 10 pegs, find all gap values from 1 to 9 for which every peg is visited, and explain what property they all share.

exercise.description: Students observe and analyse thread-art diagrams with different peg counts and thread-gaps. They predict which combinations visit all pegs (co-prime pairs) versus only some pegs (non-co-prime pairs) and create their own diagrams for four specified peg/gap combinations.

items.prompt: A school has 360 students. The principal wants to divide them into equal groups where each group size is greater than 1. She also wants to check whether groups of 24 students each are possible. Using prime factorisation, find all possible group sizes and determine whether groups of 24 are possible.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Prime factorisation of 360: 360 = 2 × 180 = 2 × 2 × 90 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 45 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 2³ × 3² × 5. The factors of 360 greater than 1 are all divisors built from these primes: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 30, 36, 40, 45, 60, 72, 90, 120, 180, 360. Prime factorisation of 24 = 2³ × 3. Since 2³ × 3 is fully contained in 2³ × 3² × 5 (360 has at least three 2s and at least one 3), 360 is divisible by 24. Groups of 24 are possible: 360 ÷ 24 = 15 groups.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Factorise 360 into primes, then check whether the prime factorisation of 24 (= 2³ × 3) is contained within it.

inclusivity.support: Build the factor tree of 360 step by step, stopping at each composite branch and splitting further until all leaves are prime.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the largest group size greater than 40 that divides 360 evenly, and show how you identified it from the prime factorisation.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.4 p.122
exercise.description: Are the following pairs co-prime? Guess first, then verify using prime factorisation: (a) 30 and 45; (b) 57 and 85; (c) 121 and 1331; (d) 343 and 216.

items.prompt: A number is formed by writing the digit 6 followed by three unknown digits: 6 _ _ _. The complete four-digit number must be divisible by both 5 and 8. Find all possible values of the last three digits and write two complete four-digit numbers that satisfy both conditions.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Divisibility by 5 requires the last digit to be 0 or 5. Divisibility by 8 requires the last three digits to form a number divisible by 8. If the last digit is 5: we need a three-digit number _ _ 5 divisible by 8. But 8 is even and any multiple of 8 is even, so it cannot end in 5. Thus the last digit must be 0. We need a three-digit number _ _ 0 divisible by 8. Multiples of 8 ending in 0: 8 × 1 = 8 (no), checking systematically: 8 × 5 = 40 (two digits), 8 × 13 = 104 (ends in 4, no), 8 × 15 = 120 ✓, 8 × 25 = 200 ✓, 8 × 35 = 280 ✓, 8 × 38 = 304 (ends in 4, no), 8 × 40 = 320 ✓, ... so valid last-three-digit endings include 120, 200, 280, 320, 360, 400, 440, 480, 520, 560, 600, 640, 680, 720, 760, 800, 840, 880, 960, 000 (=1000, too large if treating as 3-digit). Two valid four-digit numbers: 6120 and 6200.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the divisibility-by-5 last-digit rule first to determine the units digit, then apply the divisibility-by-8 last-three-digits rule.

inclusivity.support: First list all two-digit and three-digit multiples of 8 that end in 0 or 5, and then check which of those also satisfy the last-digit rule for 5.
inclusivity.challenge: How many distinct four-digit numbers of the form 6 _ _ _ are divisible by both 5 and 8? List the pattern you notice in their last three digits.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 5.5 p.125
exercise.description: 2024 is a leap year. Leap years are multiples of 4, except multiples of 100 that are not multiples of 400. (a) From your birth year to now, which years were leap years? (b) From 2024 to 2099, how many leap years are there?

items.prompt: Without performing full division, find the prime factorisation of 560 × 81 and use it to determine which of the following numbers divide 560 × 81 exactly: (a) 8, (b) 5, (c) 27, (d) 10.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 560 = 2⁴ × 5 × 7 and 81 = 3⁴. So 560 × 81 = 2⁴ × 3⁴ × 5 × 7. (a) 8 = 2³. Since 2⁴ contains 2³, yes, 8 divides 560 × 81. (b) 5 = 5¹. Since 5¹ is present, yes, 5 divides 560 × 81. (c) 27 = 3³. Since 3⁴ contains 3³, yes, 27 divides 560 × 81. (d) 10 = 2 × 5. Both 2 and 5 are present, yes, 10 divides 560 × 81.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the prime factorisation of each number separately, combine for the product, then check inclusion of each divisor's prime factorisation.

inclusivity.support: Build a factor tree for 560 and a separate one for 81, then list all the prime factors together to form the product's factorisation.
inclusivity.challenge: Find the smallest number greater than 1 that does NOT divide 560 × 81 and explain why using prime factorisations.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 5.4 p.120
exercise.description: Find the prime factorisation without multiplying first: (a) 56 × 25; (b) 108 × 75; (c) 1000 × 81.

items.prompt: Consider the set of four numbers {4, 9, 15, 17}. For each number, write one property that makes it different from the other three in the set, using ideas from this chapter. Your four properties should each be distinct.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Many valid responses exist. One possible set: 17 — the only prime number in the set; 4 — the only perfect square (2²) or the only number whose prime factorisation uses just one prime repeated (2²); 9 — also a perfect square (3²), but as 4 is already identified, 9 could be the only odd perfect square; 15 — the only number with two distinct prime factors (3 and 5) and no repeated prime. Alternatively: 4 = 2², the only even number; 9 = 3², the only odd perfect square; 15 = 3 × 5, the only composite that is not a perfect square; 17, the only prime. Students should use vocabulary: prime, composite, perfect square, prime factorisation, factors.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply chapter concepts — prime, composite, perfect square, prime factorisation — to identify a unique classifying property for each number relative to the set.

inclusivity.support: Find the prime factorisation of each number first, then compare the four factorisations and look for the one that is unlike the others.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a second valid property for the number 9 that is different from the one you used, and explain why both properties are correct but distinct.

exercise.description: In each box of four numbers, explain how each number is special compared to the others. Share and compare reasons with classmates. Boxes include: {9, 16, 25, 43}; {5, 7, 3, 8}; {27, 3, 17, 27}; {12, 35, 11, 24}; {123, 31, 44, 65}.

items.prompt: In a Prime Puzzle, a 2 × 2 grid must be filled with prime numbers so that the product of the first row is 15, the product of the second row is 14, the product of the first column is 21, and the product of the second column is 10. Find the four prime numbers that fill the grid.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Row \ Col | Col 1 | Col 2 | Row Product |
|---|---|---|---|
| Row 1 | ? | ? | 15 |
| Row 2 | ? | ? | 14 |
| Col Product | 21 | 10 | |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1 product = 15 = 3 × 5, so the two primes in row 1 are 3 and 5. Row 2 product = 14 = 2 × 7, so the two primes in row 2 are 2 and 7. Column 1 product = 21 = 3 × 7. We need one number from row 1 and one from row 2 multiplying to 21. From {3,5} and {2,7}: 3 × 7 = 21 ✓. So column 1 is 3 (row 1) and 7 (row 2), and column 2 is 5 (row 1) and 2 (row 2). Check: column 2 product = 5 × 2 = 10 ✓. Grid: top-left = 3, top-right = 5, bottom-left = 7, bottom-right = 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Factorise each row product into exactly two primes, then assign them to columns by checking that each column product constraint is satisfied.

inclusivity.support: Start by writing the prime factorisation of each row product (15 and 14) to find the only two primes that multiply to each product, then check the column products.
inclusivity.challenge: Design your own 2 × 2 Prime Puzzle by choosing four primes, computing the row and column products, and verifying that the puzzle has a unique solution.

exercise.description: Fill grids with prime numbers so that the product of each row equals the number to its right and the product of each column equals the number below it. Two grids provided (3×3 and larger). Sub-parts: (a) solve the first puzzle; (b) solve the second larger puzzle.
